papers.title: Escape Time with Quenched Extrinsic Fluctuations in Positive Feedback Systems
papers.abstract: Gene regulatory networks with positive feedback often exhibit multiple stable steady states representing distinct cellular phenotypes, allowing stochastic fluctuations to drive phenotypic switching between basins of attraction. Such transitions are commonly characterized by escape-time statistics. While previous studies have typically analyzed intrinsic fluctuation or dynamical environmental fluctuation separately, the combined effect of intrinsic biochemical fluctuation and quenched (slowly varying) extrinsic cell-to-cell parameter heterogeneity on population-level switching dynamics remains less understood. In this study, we formulate a theoretical framework to compute escape-time moments by combining the backward chemical Fokker--Planck equation with population averaging over a stationary distribution of kinetic parameters. We apply this approach to two paradigmatic bistable motifs---positive autoregulation and the genetic Toggle Switch---and quantify how quenched extrinsic heterogeneity modifies switching times across a population of autonomous cells. Our results show that extrinsic parameter variability can substantially alter the mean switching time and, more prominently, increase its dispersion, producing highly heterogeneous switching kinetics across genetically identical cells. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for cell-to-cell parameter heterogeneity when characterizing stochastic phenotypic switching in biological populations.

papers.title: From the Deterministic Hook Effect to Stochastic Reliability in Ternary Complex Formation
papers.abstract: Ternary binding systems occur in signaling, scaffold-mediated assembly, and targeted protein degradation. A mediator brings two partners into a productive ternary complex, but excess mediator can hold them in separate binary complexes. Consequently, ternary complex formation can increase and then decrease as the mediator dose increases, producing the hook effect. Deterministic dose-response curves describe the average behavior but do not indicate whether individual small compartments reliably form the complex. A minimal reversible binding network was studied using deterministic equations, exact stochastic simulations, and a simple catalytic extension. The deterministic model recovered the hook-shaped response. In stochastic simulations, small volumes often failed to accumulate the required number of complexes, even where the deterministic prediction was favorable. At low mediator doses, failure reflected a shortage of mediator molecules; at high doses, material accumulated in free or binary-bound forms. Larger volumes increased the range of mediator doses supporting reliable formation, while stricter copy-number thresholds narrowed that range. Faster ternary-complex completion or slower breakup improved reliability. In the catalytic model, product formation also depended on how early productive complexes formed. These results show why a favorable average binding response does not necessarily ensure reliable assembly in small reaction volumes.
